summary: Defines a Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) package for bulk auditing. Base MGCP audits one endpoint at a time. The bulk package lets a Call Agent learn a group's endpoint naming convention, the list of instantiated endpoints, and connection and endpoint state in fewer steps.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of knocking on every classroom door to ask who is inside, the principal gets one list of all rooms and who is in them. This makes checking a whole group of phone gateways much faster.

subtitle: A faster way to check the status of many phone gateway endpoints at once

tldr.problem: The base MGCP protocol can audit telephone gateway endpoints one at a time, which is slow when a gateway manages hundreds or thousands of endpoints, especially during system recovery.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3624 defines a bulk audit package that lets a Call Agent query a whole group of endpoints in one command, retrieving endpoint names, connection counts, connection modes, and endpoint state all at once.
tldr.outcome: The bulk package reduces the number of round-trips needed to learn the state of a gateway during failover, making recovery faster and more efficient.

today: RFC 3624 is an Informational document describing a non-IETF protocol extension that was deployed in several products. The document notes that RFC 3015 (Megaco/H.248) is the standardized alternative for media gateway control.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Media Gateway Control Protocol (MGCP) separates call control from media delivery in voice networks. A Call Agent (the controller) audits endpoints on a media gateway to learn their current state.

The base MGCP protocol's audit commands work on one endpoint at a time. For large gateways with many endpoints, this becomes inefficient, especially during failover when the system needs to quickly learn the state of hundreds or thousands of active endpoints. RFC 3624 adds a bulk audit package to solve this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: MGCP controls phone lines through a gateway. The base protocol can check one line at a time, which is slow when there are many lines.

sections.title: Bulk Audit Package Features
sections.content:
The bulk audit package (named BA) provides several audit types in a single command:

EndpointNameList: Returns the naming convention for a group of endpoints, describing which endpoint names exist (e.g., ds/ds1-[1-84]/[1-24] for T1 lines). For virtual endpoints, this shows the naming pattern even if specific instances are not active.

InstantiatedEndpointList: Returns the actual endpoints that are currently active. For virtual endpoints that come and go, this differs from the naming convention.

ConnectionCountList: Shows how many active connections exist on each endpoint in hexadecimal (0-F) or Z (more than 15).

ConnectionModeList: Indicates the connection mode (inactive, sendonly, recvonly, sendrecv, conference, loopback, etc.) for each connection on each endpoint.

EndpointStateList: Reports whether each endpoint is in-service (True), in an idle state (False), or out-of-service.
sections.plainLanguage: The bulk audit asks for several kinds of information at once: what endpoints exist, how many calls are on each, what mode each call is in, and whether endpoints are working.

sections.title: How Bulk Auditing Works
sections.content:
A bulk audit request includes optional parameters to limit scope: BA/SE specifies the starting endpoint name and BA/NU specifies the maximum number of endpoints to report in one response.

The Call Agent makes a bulk audit request with a BulkRequestedInfo parameter listing what to return (e.g., BA/F: BA/C, BA/M for connection counts and modes). The gateway responds with the requested information for the endpoint group.

If the response would be too large, the gateway can return a shortened report with BA/NE indicating the next endpoint name to query, allowing the Call Agent to continue auditing in chunks.

For virtual endpoints that may be disjoint (like endpoints 1-3 and 6-12 existing, but 4-5 not instantiated), the response includes BA/EL to specify which endpoints each result set covers.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for a group starting at a certain line and specify what you want to know. The gateway tells you, and if there is too much, you can ask for the next batch.

sections.title: Endpoint State Conditions
sections.content:
The BA/S (EndpointStateList) parameter accepts state type conditions:

I = in-service, D = disconnected, N = in notification state, L = in lockstep (waiting for request after notification), S = active on-off or timeout signal, H = not idle (off-hook for phone endpoints or non-idle for CAS/digital signaling).

The result returns True if any condition matches and the endpoint is in-service, False if none match and the endpoint is in-service, or Out of Service for endpoints that are out of service.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for endpoints in specific states, like 'which lines are disconnected' or 'which ones have an active signal', and get back True, False, or Out of Service for each.

sections.title: Practical Examples
sections.content:
Example 1: Audit all E1 endpoint names. Request: AUEP *@gw1.net / BA/F: BA/Z. Response: ba/z: ds/e1-3/[1-30] (a 30-channel E1 line).

Example 2: Get connection counts for specific endpoints. Request: AUEP ds/e1-3/* / BA/F: BA/C. Response: ba/el: ds/e1-3/[1-30], ba/c: 012111210001... (hex digits showing connection counts).

Example 3: Check endpoint state for in-service endpoints only. Request: AUEP ds/ds3-1/* / BA/F: BA/S(I), BA/SE: ds/ds3-1/ds1-6/4, BA/NU: 12. Response: ba/el: ds/ds3-1/ds1-6/[4-15], ba/s: TOOTTOOTTOOT (T = true, O = out of service).
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask 'what E1 lines exist', 'how many calls are on E1-3', or 'which lines in a range are in-service', and get compact answers back.
